# Hartwell Supply Co.: what you're looking at

Hartwell is a family-held HVAC/R distributor: about 150 people, twelve branches (Columbus, Cleveland, Cincinnati, Dayton, Toledo, Akron, Indianapolis, Fort Wayne, Louisville, Lexington, Troy MI and Pittsburgh), selling equipment, parts, refrigerant and supplies to heating and cooling contractors. The records run from 2016 to 2025.

**Its systems, each a separate database copied into the warehouse:**
- **ERP** (`erp_*`): customers and their account managers, the sales reps, products and vendors, sales orders and their lines (how each order arrived and who keyed it), purchase orders, transfers between branches, and returns.
- **Warehouse management** (`wms_*`): every stock movement (opening balances, receipts, sales, transfers, returns) and goods receipts. Stock on hand isn't stored anywhere: it's the running total of the movements.
- **Accounting** (`finance_*`): invoices and their lines, credit memos, customer payments, vendor bills and their lines, and vendor payments.
- **CRM** (`crm_*`): calls and emails to customer service, as logged by whoever took them; and the reps' quotes, with each quote's lines, its outcome (won, lost or expired), a loss reason when the rep entered one, and the order a won quote became.
- **External** (`external_*`): real monthly heating and cooling degree days and residential building permits for each branch's county.

**Days.** `day` is an operating day, about 21 a month; `dim_date` gives the calendar date.

**What isn't here:** profitability by customer, rep or branch; why a return happened; whether an order was keyed correctly; whether a vendor bill was right. Like any real business, those have to be worked out from the records, and some of them can't be.

WITH x AS (SELECT po.purpose, d.year, (l.qty>p.qty) qo, l.qty*l.unit_cost-p.qty*p.unit_cost diff, p.qty*p.unit_cost pv
FROM finance_vendor_bill_lines l JOIN finance_vendor_bills b USING(bill_id)
JOIN erp_purchase_order_lines p ON p.po_id=b.po_id AND p.sku=l.sku JOIN erp_purchase_orders po ON po.po_id=b.po_id
JOIN dim_date d ON d.day=b.day
JOIN finance_vendor_payments vp ON vp.bill_id=b.bill_id AND abs(vp.amount-b.amount)<0.01)
SELECT year,
 round(sum(diff) FILTER (WHERE diff>0.005),2) excess,
 round(sum(diff) FILTER (WHERE diff>0.005 AND qo AND purpose='stock'),2) a_stock_qty,
 round(sum(diff) FILTER (WHERE diff>0.005 AND qo AND purpose='special'),2) b_special_qty,
 round(sum(diff) FILTER (WHERE diff>0.005 AND NOT qo),2) c_cost_only,
 round(sum(pv),2) po_value,
 round(sum(diff) FILTER (WHERE diff>0.005)/10,2) excess_per_yr_10,
 round(sum(diff) FILTER (WHERE diff>0.005 AND qo AND purpose='stock')/10,2) a_per_yr_10,
 round(sum(diff) FILTER (WHERE diff>0.005 AND qo AND purpose='special')/10,2) b_per_yr_10,
 round(sum(diff) FILTER (WHERE diff>0.005 AND NOT qo)/10,2) c_per_yr_10,
 round(100*sum(diff) FILTER (WHERE diff>0.005)/sum(pv),4) excess_pct_of_po
FROM x GROUP BY ROLLUP(year) ORDER BY year NULLS LAST

content.text:
The challenge was right on every point, so I've accepted it and saved a narrower F2 to `finding.json` (`accepted: true`). Over 2016–2025 Hartwell paid $3,166,564.74 more than PO value on 13,949 bills paid in full, about $316,656.47 a year (q231). That amount is what was paid, and stays the headline. How much of it can be shown to be wrong is now much smaller:

| Part | 10-year total | Per year | Evidence |
|---|---|---|---|
| (a) Extra quantity billed on stock POs | 847,795.65 | 84,779.56 | **Proven not received.** Every billed stock line has a warehouse receipt equal to the PO quantity (q164). |
| (b) Extra quantity billed on special orders | 1,498,042.39 | 149,804.24 | **Not provable.** Special orders have no warehouse receipt at all. Indirect check: on all 1,228 of 1,290 lines that match exactly one customer sale, the customer got the PO quantity, never the billed quantity (q193). That fits non-delivery but doesn't prove it. |
| (c) Higher unit cost on otherwise matching quantity | 820,726.70 | 82,072.67 | **Can't judge.** PO cost equals the product master cost on every line and never changed for any SKU in ten years, so the PO isn't a real price reference (q171, q183). |

What changed after the challenge:
- **Vendor credits:** my earlier credit test was a join error. Matched correctly, all 1,234 credits trace to goods returned to vendors (q169). Nothing offsets the excess, so I withdrew the $273,967.29 floor.
- **Price increase:** my "no price increase" test is now weak evidence, because PO prices never move.
- **Short-pays:** AP paid exactly PO value, without freight, on about 30% of all bills that differed from the PO for any reason. That includes 6,115 of 20,329 bills where only freight differed (q202). So it looks like a pay-to-PO rule applied to some bills, not a check that catches overbills. Some of the withheld freight may have been owed.
- **Recovery window:** claims should start with 2024–2025, which carry $658,006.40 of excess, $157,039.15 of it proven unreceived stock quantity (q187, q234). Older bills are probably past any practical dispute window, though the data has no contract terms to confirm that.
- **Confidence:** now high for the amount paid above PO and for (a), medium for (b), low for (c).

The challenger also found a separate issue: second bills paid on POs that were billed twice, $2,732,286.38 in total (q172). I've listed it as a next step, not added it to F2's figure.

The challenger computed (a) per year as 84,779.57 (q207) and my re-run gives 84,779.56; the difference is rounding.
